draft.title: Pompeii
card: Pompeii was a Roman town near the Bay of Naples, in Italy. In 79 CE the volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried it under ash and pumice.
The ash covered the town quickly and sealed it. Homes, shops, wall paintings and street signs were preserved for almost 1700 years.
Scribbled graffiti on walls shows what ordinary people said and thought. Bakeries, bars and workshops show how people earned a living.
Many victims were buried in ash that later hardened. The bodies rotted away and left hollow shapes. Archaeologists filled these with plaster to show how people looked and where they died.
draft.remember: Pompeii is a sealed snapshot of Roman daily life, preserved by the ash that buried it.

a.q: Why is Pompeii so useful to historians who study everyday Roman life?
opts: Ash buried the town fast and preserved ordinary buildings
Its Senate records describe the whole Roman Republic
Soldiers wrote about it in detail after the eruption
Rome rebuilt it exactly as it had been before 79 CE
a.why: The ash sealed the town and kept homes, shops and graffiti much as they were. That gives direct evidence of ordinary life. The town was not rebuilt, so it is not a later copy.
a.clue: Think about what the ash did to the town.

b.q: An archaeologist finds scratched writing on a wall in Pompeii that complains about the price of bread. What does it show about Roman life?
opts: Ordinary people wrote their opinions about daily matters
Only rich Romans could write messages in public places
Bread was the only food sold in Pompeii
The town was already empty before the eruption
b.why: Graffiti was written by ordinary people, so a complaint about bread shows what they cared about. One wall message cannot show that bread was the only food sold. It also does not show that the town was empty.
b.clue: Who would scribble a complaint on a wall?

a.best: Ash buried the town fast and preserved ordinary buildings

b.best: Ordinary people wrote their opinions about daily matters

problems.detail: 'Street signs' is misleading. Pompeii's streets did not carry name signs as modern streets do. What survived were painted notices, election slogans and shop signs. 'Painted notices' or 'shop signs' would be accurate.
